title: the courage not to strike
hook: the yoga list that starts before any pose: not-harming
carry: do no harm — start with your mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti, love practiced like an instrument. Your line was devotion is a verb. Did you do the loving thing on a day you didn't feel like it? Today's word asks for a different kind of strength. Day seventeen.

A message comes in late at night. It's unfair, and it stings, and your thumbs already know the reply. The sharp one. The one that would land. Here's a strange fact about yoga. Before the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali teach anything about posture, they set out a short list of restraints, the ground the rest is built on, and the first word on that list isn't stretch, or breathe. It's not-harming. So the first restraint in that text has something to say to those thumbs.
screen: `A MESSAGE. A SHARP REPLY READY.` → `YOGA BEFORE THE POSES.` → `THE FIRST WORD: NOT-HARMING.`

segments.voice: Ahimsa. Himsa is harm, violence. Ahimsa is its opposite: not-harming. And it's easy to hear that as a soft word, a word for people who never stand up for anything. Gandhi, who put this word beside truth at the center of his public life, heard it the other way around. He was not a quiet man. He confronted an empire, and he refused the one weapon everyone expected him to pick up. Ahimsa takes nerve. When something hits a person, the body often wants to hit back, and ahimsa is the half-second where you don't add more harm to a moment that already has some. The Jains, close neighbors on the same soil, hold ahimsa at the heart of their path too. Now look at what Patanjali says comes of it. The Yoga Sutras teach that when someone is truly settled in not-harming, hostility falls away in their presence. Not because they won the argument. Because they stopped feeding it. Some teachers name three places ahimsa lives: in thought, in word, and in deed. Deeds are the obvious ones. Today's line starts with the middle one, words, because that's where the half-second is easiest to miss. The cutting joke. The thing said about someone who isn't in the room. The reply sent at night. One more layer. The vow points inward too. A voice in the head that calls a person worthless is himsa as well. Not-harming includes the one doing the not-harming.
screen: `AHIMSA — NOT-HARMING.` · `NOT SOFT. IT TAKES NERVE.` · `HOSTILITY FALLS AWAY.` · `THOUGHT, WORD, DEED.` · then, large: `START WITH YOUR MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Now, find the half-second. Bring back the last time you said something sharp, to someone or about someone. Don't punish yourself for it; that would be harm too. Just replay it, slowly, and this time stop at the moment before the words came out. Feel the push to strike. Let it pass through without acting on it. What could have been said instead? Maybe nothing. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Ahimsa. Not-harming, in thought, word and deed. The courage not to strike. Seventeenth word.
Your line: do no harm — start with your mouth. Today, let one sharp sentence go unsaid, and notice what happens to the room. Day seventeen.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY THE WORLD LOOKS SOLID.`

howItsDone: In Hindu life ahimsa shows up in vegetarian kitchens, care for animals and restraint in speech, and yoga teachers present it as the first of the restraints in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

what a scholar hears: Yoga Sutras 2.30 lists ahimsa first among the restraints (yamas); 2.35 says hostility is given up in the presence of one established in it.

notes: Yoga Sutras 2.30 (ahimsa first of the yamas) and 2.35 (hostility abandoned in the presence of one established in ahimsa) paraphrased; confirm sutra numbers and wording.
'Himsa is harm; ahimsa is its opposite' is given as a definition, not a root study; confirm.

Gandhi and the Jains named briefly as people who held ahimsa central; manuscript's salt-march dates, distances and crowd numbers cut under the claims rule. Confirm the Gandhi framing ('confronted an empire') is acceptable.
'Teachers often name three places: thought, word and deed' (manasa, vacha, karmana) is a common teaching formula, not tied to a cited verse here; confirm or suggest a source.
howItsDone mentions vegetarianism as one expression of ahimsa; confirm phrasing.

Editor pass: 'long before any pose' and 'the very first thing the text asks' overstated the order of the Sutras (2.30 lists ahimsa first among the yamas; posture comes at 2.46), now 'before they say a word about posture' and 'the first restraint'; 'the tradition hears it' reattributed to Gandhi; 'teachers often' made 'some teachers'; 'for a lot of us the harm we do comes out of the mouth' and 'the voice in your own head' cut so the narrator no longer tells the listener about themselves.

Audit (2026-10-01): 'before the Yoga Sutras say a word about posture' was still inexact, since 2.29 names asana in the list of eight limbs just before 2.30; now 'before they teach anything about posture' (posture is taught at 2.46). Gandhi framing made 'beside truth' (he paired ahimsa with satya); 'the whole body wants to hit back' softened to 'often'.
Editor review 2: hook's last line ('which means the first restraint in the text is about those thumbs, right now') was garbled and overclaimed; rewritten. Practice opener varied.
